paragraphs: 1 Now Jacob looked up and saw Esau coming toward him with four hundred men. So he divided the children among Leah, Rachel, and the two maidservants. 2 He put the maidservants and their children in front, Leah and her children next, and Rachel and Joseph at the rear. 3 But Jacob himself went on ahead and bowed to the ground seven times as he approached his brother.
4 Esau, however, ran to him and embraced him, threw his arms around his neck, and kissed him. And they both wept.
5 When Esau looked up and saw the women and children, he asked, “Who are these with you?”

Jacob answered, “These are the children God has graciously given your servant.” 6 Then the maidservants and their children approached and bowed down. 7 Leah and her children also approached and bowed down, and then Joseph and Rachel approached and bowed down.
8 “What do you mean by sending this whole company to meet me?” asked Esau.
“To find favor in your sight, my lord,” Jacob answered.
9 “I already have plenty, my brother,” Esau replied. “Keep what belongs to you.”

10 But Jacob insisted, “No, please! If I have found favor in your sight, then receive this gift from my hand. For indeed, I have seen your face, and it is like seeing the face of God, since you have received me favorably. 11 Please accept my gift that was brought to you, because God has been gracious to me and I have all I need.” So Jacob pressed him until he accepted.
12 Then Esau said, “Let us be on our way, and I will go ahead of you.”

13 But Jacob replied, “My lord knows that the children are frail, and I must care for sheep and cattle that are nursing their young. If they are driven hard for even a day, all the animals will die. 14 Please let my lord go ahead of his servant. I will continue on slowly, at a comfortable pace for the livestock and children, until I come to my lord at Seir.”
15 “Let me leave some of my people with you,” Esau said.
But Jacob replied, “Why do that? Let me find favor in the sight of my lord.”
16 So that day Esau started on his way back to Seir, 17 but Jacob went on to Succoth, where he built a house for himself and shelters for his livestock; that is why the place was called Succoth.

context_lines: Esau arrives with the four hundred men Jacob feared. Jacob arranges the family with the maidservants and their children first, Leah and her children next, and Rachel and Joseph last. He himself goes ahead of them, bowing as he approaches his brother. The unequal order of the household remains visible, but Jacob faces the meeting first.

Esau runs to embrace and kiss him, and both brothers weep. Instead of the attack Jacob feared, he receives a welcome. As Esau asks about the family, Jacob describes the children as gifts God has graciously given him, and they come forward to meet their uncle.

The brothers then discuss the livestock gifts. Esau says he has enough and does not need them, but Jacob presses him to accept. He links the welcome with God's favor and acknowledges that God has been gracious to him. The gift can now be received within a restored relationship rather than remaining only an attempt to prevent an attack.

Esau offers to travel with Jacob, but Jacob points to the needs of the children and nursing animals and declines an escort. Esau returns to Seir, while Jacob goes to Succoth and builds shelters. The narrative records their peaceful parting without describing every later visit or conversation between them.
common_interpretation_lines: A common Christian reading emphasizes reconciliation, unexpected kindness, and Jacob's recognition of God's grace in his brother's welcome. [Wesley's notes on Genesis 33:3–12](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/) connect the brothers' peace with God's care and regard Jacob's concern for the traveling household as appropriate.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
god_plan_lines: The welcome offers a helpful parallel to the larger biblical theme of reconciliation. Jacob approaches afraid of what his past has left between them, and he finds an embrace. [Wesley, on Genesis 33:10](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/), already reads Jacob's comparison with seeing God's face in terms of restored peace.

At the greater level, [2 Corinthians 5:18–21](https://biblehub.com/bsb/2_corinthians/5.htm) says that God reconciles people to Himself through Christ. [Ephesians 2:8–10](https://biblehub.com/bsb/ephesians/2.htm) distinguishes salvation as God's gift from the good works that follow it. Read alongside that theme, Jacob's insistence on giving after being welcomed helps illustrate generosity as a response to grace, rather than a payment that creates it.
